Interoceptive AI · pre-registered plan and results · 2026-09-07

Does the Modulator Listen Inward?

Sixteen agents, differing in what a small second network is allowed to read and which parts of the policy it is allowed to re-tune. This page is the plan for reading them — what was measured, why those measures and not the obvious one, and what would have to be true for the answer to be believed — followed by the answer, which is that none of the sixteen behaved differently from an agent with no second network at all.

The question, and the measure that cannot answer it

The agent carries a second, small network — the neuromodulator — that reads its senses and continuously re-tunes the main policy, the way a brain chemical such as acetylcholine re-tunes cortex. The claim the project is built on is not that a modulated agent behaves differently. It is sharper than that: that a modulated agent's response to the outside world should vary more with its internal state — that being hurt should change how it reads a predator, not merely change what it does.

That is an interaction, not a main effect, and it is what everything below is built to measure.

The one thing that changes what you asked for

You asked for an internal-state-dependent bush hiding comparison. Bush hiding is the measure this project has used for a year, and a recent analysis showed it is largely a by-product rather than a decision.

A wounded agent mostly freezes to heal. Its Rest rate rises by 17.7 to 35.2 percentage points — about five times the size of the bush-hiding effect — and that resting happens mostly in the open. Whether freezing registers as “hides more” depends only on whether the agent happened to be standing on a bush when it stopped. Across fourteen agents, “hides more when injured” was positive in 13 of 14 over the first 25 steps, 2 of 14 over the first 100, and 1 of 14 over the whole episode. The sign is a property of the window and of where cover happens to be, not of a decision.

So bush hiding stays in the battery — it is the historical measure and dropping it would break comparability with every earlier study — but it is demoted. It cannot carry the headline, and a modulator that changes it has not yet been shown to have changed anything the agent decided.

The escape is to score a movement decision instead of a location. An agent that freezes then contributes nothing in either direction: freezing removes the step from the denominator rather than loading it into the numerator. That measure already exists, is already pre-registered for this grid, and is described in the battery below as B0.

Words this page uses

Every term below appears later on. Open the ones you need; skip the rest. Nothing here is required reading if the vocabulary is already familiar.

The agent and its body

Interoceptive — sensing your own body from the inside

Interoception is the sense of your own internal condition: hunger, pain, how hard your heart is working. It is the counterpart of exteroception, which is sensing the outside world through eyes, ears and nose. This agent has both. Its interoceptive channels report how injured it is, how hungry it is, and a pain-like signal; its exteroceptive channels report what it can see, smell and bump into.

The whole project is named for this distinction, and this experiment is the first that can switch one off and leave the other on.

Nociception, and why it is not called pain — the raw damage signal

Nociception is the detection of tissue damage — the signal a nerve sends when something harmful happens. Pain is the experience that may or may not follow from it. Keeping the two apart is not pedantry here: pain is the thing this project is trying to explain, so calling the input “pain” would assume the conclusion. The agent has a nociceptor; whether anything pain-like emerges is the open question.

The agent's nociceptor is also delayed and smoothed. It does not report the wound directly; it reports a weighted average of the last twelve steps of damage, which means an agent that wakes up badly hurt feels nothing at all for two steps and does not feel the full wound until step twelve. Several findings in this project turn on that delay.

Bush hiding — the fraction of steps spent standing in cover

The world contains bushes that conceal the agent from predators. Bush hiding is simply the share of an episode's steps the agent spent standing in one. It has been this project's main behavioural measure for about a year, which is why it appears here at all — and why the finding that it is mostly a by-product of freezing, rather than a decision to hide, mattered enough to change this plan's headline measure.

Survival steps — how long the agent stayed alive

Performance in this project is always measured in survival steps, never in accumulated reward. Reward is what the agent is trained on; survival is what we actually care about, and the two can come apart. An agent can learn to farm reward in ways that do not keep it alive longer.

The modulator

Neuromodulator (the “NMN”) — a small network that re-tunes the big one

The agent's decisions come from one main network. Alongside it sits a much smaller second network that reads the agent's senses and, at every step, adjusts how the main network processes what it sees. The biological analogy is a neuromodulator such as acetylcholine or noradrenaline: a chemical that does not carry the message itself but changes how the rest of the brain handles it.

The point is not that a modulated agent does different things. It is that a modulated agent should respond to the same outside cue differently depending on its internal state — that being hurt should change how it reads a predator.

FiLM — the specific way the re-tuning is done

Short for Feature-wise Linear Modulation. For every neuron in the layer being modulated, the modulator produces two numbers: a gain to multiply that neuron's output by, and an offset to add to it. That is the entire operation — multiply and add, per neuron.

It matters here because until this week different modulation sites in this codebase used different operations, so “where the modulator acts” was tangled up with “how it acts”. A companion refactor made every site use FiLM, which is what finally allows the two to be varied separately.

Site, and the five row labels — which part of the policy gets re-tuned

The main network is a pipeline: senses go in, get encoded, pass through a memory cell, and come out as an action choice and a value estimate. The modulator can be attached at any of those places, and the grid's rows are exactly that choice.

t2enc re-tunes the sensory front-end, where raw senses are first processed. t3rnn re-tunes the memory cell, which carries information across steps. t4act re-tunes the action layers, which choose what to do. t5crt re-tunes the value head, which estimates how good the situation is. t16quad re-tunes all four at once, and t1none is the control with no modulator at all.

I, X and ALL — which senses the modulator is allowed to read

I is interoceptive only: the modulator sees the body's own channels — injury, hunger, the nociceptive signal — and nothing of the outside world. X is exteroceptive only: sight, smell, collision, and nothing of the body. ALL is everything, which is what the modulator has always read until now.

This is the axis the project's thesis rests on, which is why the results section leads with the I-versus-X comparison rather than with a ranking of sites.

How the measuring works

Percentage points (pp) — why not just “percent”

If a rate goes from 20% to 25%, that is a rise of five percentage points, but a rise of twenty-five percent relative to where it started. Both are true and they are different numbers. This page always uses percentage points for changes in a rate, so that a change is never confused with a proportion of a change.

Randomised starting injury — and why it is the only honest thing to bin on

At the start of every episode the environment deals the agent a wound drawn at random, before the agent has done anything. That number is causally identified: because it was assigned at random, any behaviour that tracks it must have been caused by it.

Contrast the injury the agent happens to be carrying at some later step. That is partly a consequence of the agent's own choices — a cautious agent gets hurt less — so a correlation between carried injury and behaviour could run in either direction. Both quantities get measured in this project, but only the randomised one supports a causal claim, and the two are kept carefully apart.

Seed, and why one is not enough — the limit that governs this whole analysis

A seed is the starting number for the random-number generator: it fixes the initial network weights and the order training data arrives in. Two runs of identical configuration with different seeds are two samples from the same distribution, and they can land far apart.

In this project they land very far apart. Five runs of one identical configuration in the immediately preceding study finished anywhere between 35.5 and 136.7 survival steps. Every cell in this grid has one seed, so a gap between two cells could be the modulator or could be the dice, and nothing in the data separates them.

Pre-registration — deciding the test before seeing the data

Writing down what will be measured, and what counts as a positive result, before looking at any of the numbers. It exists because a threshold chosen after seeing the data is not a test: with enough measures and enough freedom to pick, something always looks significant.

It is why this page's results section is empty and must stay empty. Once a number from this grid has been looked at, nothing in the plan above may be revised without a dated note saying what changed and why, with the original left visible.

Episode, and checkpoint — one life, and a saved snapshot

An episode is one life: the agent spawns into a freshly randomised world, acts until it dies or runs out of time, and the world resets. Training here runs for ten million of them.

A checkpoint is a saved copy of the network partway through training. They are written periodically, so a run that has reached 9.4 million episodes has roughly forty-seven of them. Comparing two agents at different checkpoints compares different amounts of training as well as different designs, which is why nothing here is computed until every cell has reached the same one.

Rest and Eat — the two actions that are not movement

The agent chooses one action per step. Four of them are moves. The other two are Rest, which holds still and lets injury heal, and Eat, which consumes food on the current square.

They matter disproportionately here. A wounded agent rests far more, and that single fact is what makes location-based measures untrustworthy: an agent that stops moving stops changing where it is, so any measure of where it is starts reporting how much it rested. The headline measure excludes both actions for exactly this reason.

Confound — two explanations the data cannot separate

A confound is a second explanation for a result that the measurement cannot rule out. If injured agents both rest more and sit in bushes more, then “injury causes hiding” and “injury causes resting, and resting happens to occur in bushes” predict the same observation, and the observation cannot tell them apart.

Most of the design decisions on this page are attempts to remove one specific confound, and most of the limits section is an admission of the ones that remain.

Quasi-binomial regression — the statistics behind the factor analysis

A way of modelling a proportion — here, the fraction of an episode's steps spent in cover — against several explanatory variables at once, so that the effect of each can be read with the others held fixed.

The quasi part matters: ordinary binomial regression assumes a specific amount of random scatter, and real episodes scatter much more than that. Left uncorrected, that makes every effect look far more certain than it is. The quasi-binomial version measures the excess scatter from the data and widens its error bars accordingly — in this project by a factor of thirteen to twenty-seven.

The trajectory store, and its row footgun — where the data lives

After training, each agent is put back into the exact world it trained in and run for a large number of episodes, and everything it did is recorded into a store of files — one row per step, plus a row for the starting state.

The footgun: row t holds the state of the world at t together with the action that arrived at t. So the action a row carries is the one that produced it, not the one chosen from it. Getting that off by one silently measures a different quantity — and has done, twice, in this project's history. Every measure on this page states which row it reads from for that reason.

What is training

Two things about the modulator have never been varied independently, because until this week the code did not allow it: what it reads, and which parts of the policy it re-tunes. A companion refactor made every re-tuning site use the same operation and made each site switchable, so “where it acts” is finally separable from “how it acts”. The grid crosses the two factors.

Why the purple column is the point

If a modulator that reads only the body produces internal-state-dependent behaviour, the project's story holds: an interoceptive signal re-tunes perception. If a modulator that reads only the outside world does just as well, the story is in trouble — whatever the modulator is doing, it is not interoception, and the same benefit was available without ever looking inward. That single contrast is worth more than any ranking of sites.

The measure battery

Four tiers, and the tier matters as much as the measure. Tier A is pre-registered: its threshold was fixed before any run in this grid existed and may not be adjusted afterwards. Everything below it is either a decomposition that explains a tier-A result or an exploratory measure that may generate a hypothesis but may not settle one.

Every measure is computed per cell and compared against the unmodulated control.

B Survival steps Does the modulator help the agent live longer? Necessary, not sufficient. A modulator can raise survival by statically re-weighting channels without ever conditioning on internal state, so this cannot carry the claim alone.

D Threat-response interaction — response to a near predator, split by injury Does being hurt change how the agent answers a threat? Exploratory, and known to be confounded. A frozen agent cannot answer a predator by moving, so the effect shrinks with injury whether or not any decision changed. Reported, never used to settle anything.
D Rabbit false-alarm shift Does injury make a harmless animal read as dangerous? Exploratory. This is the sharpest available form of the hypervigilance claim, but the earlier study found the effect lives on the odour channel rather than the proximity channel, so it needs its own care.

What B0 actually is

The exact computation — open if you will be checking or reproducing this

Written out because the store's row convention has bitten this project before — row t holds the world at t together with the action that arrived at t, so an entry event straddles two rows:

← this block is wider than the column here — scroll it sideways

# denominator: the agent was standing in the open and chose to MOVE
#              (not Rest, not Eat)
denominator:  agent_in_bush[t]   == False
              action[t+1]        in {0,1,2,3}

# numerator: that move landed it in cover
numerator:    agent_in_bush[t+1] == True

# binned by the injury the environment dealt at t = 0, before the agent acted --
# the only internal-state variable that is causally identified
binned by:    injury[t = 0]

Binning on the randomised starting injury rather than the injury the agent happens to be carrying is what makes the comparison causal rather than associational. An agent's carried injury is partly a consequence of its own behaviour; the wound it was dealt at reset is not.

In one sentence, without the notation: of the times the agent was standing in the open and decided to take a step, how often did that step put it into cover — and does that fraction change depending on how badly it woke up hurt?

Where each measure comes from

You asked which previous analysis was for this. Every measure above is inherited — none of it is new, and that is deliberate. The value here is the combination, applied to a design that varies the one factor none of the earlier studies could.

What would make this wrong

Stated before any number exists, because a limit disclosed after a result reads as an excuse.

One seed per cell — the limit that governs everything else

Sixteen cells at one seed each gives a number for every combination and a confidence interval for none. The immediately preceding study ran five seeds of one identical configuration and they finished between 35.5 and 136.7 survival steps. A gap of that size between two cells of this grid could be the modulator or could be the seed, and nothing in the data distinguishes them.

The consequence is asymmetric, and it is the part worth internalising: a cell that wins is protected, because the design requires it to be re-run at five seeds before anyone may call it an effect. A cell that loses is not protected. A site that would work fine, handed one unlucky seed, gets recorded as “does not help” and dropped — and nobody re-runs a negative. This analysis will therefore report no eliminations. A cell that fails to clear a threshold will be reported as untested, not as refuted.

Four narrower threats, each with what is actually done about it

  • Every cell must reach the same checkpoint before anything is computed. Comparing a cell stopped at 8.2 million episodes against one that reached 10 million would confound the modulator with the budget. Satisfied: all sixteen finished within 105 episodes of ten million, and no measure was computed until they had.
  • The store's identity hash is not a same-world check. It hashes the whole resolved config including the seed and the run tag, so it differs across runs whose environment is identical. A reader who treats it as a pairing check will wrongly conclude the comparison is invalid. Pairing is established empirically instead — by confirming the animal draws, observation draws, starting injury and spawn cell are bit-identical across shared episode seeds.
  • One action index cannot be verified from the store. B0's denominator excludes both Rest and Eat. Rest has a witness column and is checked on every store; Eat does not, and is taken from the source. If the action ordering ever changed, Rest would fail loudly and Eat would fail silently. Stated because it is not fixable from the data, only bounded.
  • A dead modulator and a useless one look identical. This is what tier C is for. Without the modulator's own internal statistics, “this site does not help” cannot be separated from “this site never learned to do anything at all”, and the second is a training result rather than a scientific one.

An open question that is yours, not mine

The experiment's own reviewer proposed spending the same sixteen slots differently: five write sites at three seeds each, then the two survivors crossed with the input slices at three seeds. That buys replication on every comparison — eliminations become trustworthy — at the cost of deferring the interoception question, the one the project's thesis rests on, by roughly fifteen hours. The grid as launched answers the thesis question immediately and cannot eliminate anything. Both are defensible; the choice is a research call rather than a technical one, and it is recorded in the design document as still open.

What gets reported, and in what order

Fixed now so that the reporting order cannot be chosen after seeing which cut looks best.

  1. Does the modulator do anything at all? Every cell against the unmodulated control, on B0 first and survival second.
  2. Body-only against world-only. The purple column against the blue one, pooled across sites. This is the thesis test and it is reported whichever way it comes out.
  3. Which site, if any. Ranked, with every difference smaller than the seed-noise floor explicitly marked as indistinguishable rather than ordered.
  4. The decomposition. Rest rate and the two halves of bush hiding, so a headline movement can be attributed to a decision or to freezing.
  5. The modulator's own behaviour. Tier C, used only to explain a null — never to rescue one.
  6. Exploratory. Tier D, labelled as such, generating hypotheses for a replicated follow-up.

1b · A correction to the numbers this page carried yesterday

Δrest was measured against a bin holding 25 rows

The rest measure took its baseline from the lowest injury bin, injury 0. The starting wound is drawn from a continuous range, so an exactly-zero wound is a measure-zero event: that bin held about 25 rows out of five million in every one of the twenty-one runs. Every Δrest reported here yesterday was a difference against a 25-sample estimate.

The headline measure was never affected — B0 applies a minimum-support guard of 2,000 rows and correctly skipped that bin. The rest measure did not, and nothing raised, because a 25-row estimate is a perfectly well-formed number.

What changes. Measured against the lowest populated bin, the five controls span 18.2 to 21.1 points rather than 8.6 to 44.9, and their standard deviation falls from 14.8 to 1.21 — a factor of thirteen. The corrected figures are below; the conclusion about the modulator is unchanged, because it never rested on this measure.

And the correction exposes a bigger problem: the registered control band may not be a control

With the noise removed, t1none sits at z = +3.4 — higher than twelve of the fifteen modulated cells. t1none is the grid's own unmodulated control, trained the same day, on the same code, with no modulator at all. It cannot be 3.4 standard deviations from an unmodulated agent because of modulation.

Twelve of the sixteen cells sit above the control mean, the control cell among them. That is a batch difference between the five reference runs (trained 2026-09-04) and the grid (2026-09-07), not an effect of anything this grid varies.

What it is not: the Monte-Carlo return path is byte-identical between the two dates — the commit in between only adds new modes — and the one config difference, lr_critic, is read by no code in the repository. Both were checked rather than assumed. The cause is still open.

The consequence is what matters. The design pre-registered those five runs as the control band. On this evidence they are not a clean control for this grid, and the only control that certainly is — t1none — is a single run. Every comparison on this page should be read against t1none, and none of them is replicated.

1c · The curves the differences were taken from

Yesterday's version of this page reported endpoint differences and nothing else. That is enough to say a number did not move and not enough to see what it was doing, so here are the curves.

Reproduce this figure: python scripts/analysis/studies/nmn_site_grid/grid_figures.py → g01_decision_vs_byproduct.png. It reads the per-run JSON written by scripts/analysis/context_dependence.py --measures all --state injury.

Data behind this figure. 21 runs of 1,000,000 episodes (100% of those collected). The bush-entry curve uses 129,246,901 of 3,537,855,984 step rows (3.7%) — the rows where the agent stood in the open, within the first 25 steps, and chose to move. The rest curve uses all first-25-step rows. The injury 0 bin is absent from both, for the reason given above: 25 rows cannot carry a rate.

Why look

The headline number of this study is a difference between the two ends of a curve — the bush-entry rate of a badly wounded agent minus that of a barely wounded one. A difference of zero can mean the curve is flat, or it can mean the curve moved in some shape that the two chosen endpoints happen to miss. Only drawing the curve distinguishes those. The same figure also settles a second question the tables cannot: whether the measure this study is built on — the decision to step into cover — is even on the same scale as the behaviour the earlier studies reported, which was the agent simply standing still.

How it is computed

Every run contributes one million evaluation episodes played with its weights frozen, and only the first 25 steps of each are used. That window exists because the starting wound is randomised at reset and then heals: after about 25 steps the agent's injury reflects what it has done rather than what it was dealt. Steps are binned by that randomised starting injury, which is what makes the comparison causal: nothing the agent did decided which bin it landed in. Top panel, bush-entry rate: of the steps where the agent stood outside a bush and chose to move, the percentage that put it inside a bush on the next row. Resting and eating are excluded from that denominator on purpose, so it scores a decision to move into cover and cannot be inflated by an agent that simply stopped moving. Middle panel, rest rate: the percentage of all first-25 steps on which it chose to rest. Bottom panel: both on one axis, unrescaled. The action on a row was chosen while the agent looked at the previous row, so the standing-in-the-open test is read at t and the arrival at t+1. A bin holding fewer than 2,000 qualifying steps is dropped, which is why injury 0 appears nowhere: the wound is drawn from a continuous range, so exactly zero occurs about 25 times in five million rows. The grey band is the range of the five reference controls, not a confidence interval.

What it shows

The two panels are not comparable events. Take each agent from its least-injured band to its most-injured one: no cell's bush-entry rate moves more than 0.35 percentage points, in either direction, while every cell's rest rate climbs by between 17.2 and 28.6 percentage points. That is a factor of roughly fifty between the behaviour this study measures and the behaviour beside it. The panel annotations say the same thing about the reference agents: across all three injury bins the five controls' bush-entry values occupy a total range of 1.2 points and their rest values 24.1. In the bottom panel, where neither is rescaled, entering cover is the nearly flat line hugging the bottom of the axis while resting climbs from about a third of all steps to well over half. Every one of the fifteen modulated cells traces the same two shapes as the unmodulated control. A wounded agent in this environment does not travel to cover; it stops moving where it already is, and cover is whatever happens to be underneath it.

Reproduce this figure: python scripts/analysis/studies/nmn_site_grid/grid_figures.py → g02_interaction_body_vs_world.png. It reads the randomised_early block of the per-run JSON written by scripts/analysis/context_dependence.py --measures all --state injury.

Data behind this figure. 10 of the 16 cells (62%) — the five body-only and five world-only cells; the five everything cells are not on these axes because the figure exists to contrast the two restricted slices, and t1none is drawn on both panels as the shared reference. Plus all five reference controls for the band. Every curve pools that run's full 1,000,000 episodes.

Why look

Figure 1 asks whether the modulator changed behaviour at all. This one asks the sharper question the project was built to answer: does it matter what the modulator is allowed to read? The whole interoceptive claim is that a signal from the body — injury, hunger, nociception — should change how the agent reacts to the world. If that claim holds, the cells whose modulator sees only body channels should behave differently from the cells whose modulator sees only world channels. Two panels on one shared y-scale is the least generous way to ask that, because a difference has nowhere to hide in a rescaling.

How it is computed

The quantity on the y-axis is a difference of two probabilities, not a rate. For each run, every step in the first 25 of an episode is labelled two ways: by the agent's randomised starting injury bin, and by whether the nearest live predator was within two cells, measured in chebyshev distance — the number of moves a chess king would need, which is the right metric because the agent also moves diagonally. Within each injury bin the analysis then computes the chance of the agent being inside a bush when a predator is that close, minus the chance when none is, and reports the difference in percentage points. A positive number means the agent is more likely to be under cover when something is hunting it. Plotting that difference against injury is what makes the figure an interaction: a flat line means the threat response does not depend on how hurt the agent is, and a rising line means it does. A cell is only plotted for a bin holding at least 20,000 steps on each side of the comparison, so a bin cannot produce a point from a handful of rows. The five reference controls are pooled the same way and drawn as a grey smallest-to-largest envelope; as elsewhere on this page that is a range and not a confidence interval, so a curve leaving it is not by itself a finding.

What it shows

Both panels climb, and they finish in the same place: at the highest injury band the five body-only cells span 13.4–15.0 percentage points and the five world-only cells span 13.7–15.2 — two ranges that essentially coincide, with the unmodulated control at 14.4 and the five reference controls covering 13.6–15.1. The one place they are not identical is the lowest injury band, where the body-only cells sit at 6.7–8.5 and the world-only cells at 9.1–11.8. That gap is real in the picture and worth naming rather than glossing, but it is not evidence of the effect this study was looking for: the five control runs alone span 7.1–10.8 at that same bin, which covers most of both groups, so the separation is no larger than the spread between five agents that have no modulator at all. And its direction is wrong for the claim — the body-reading cells respond less to a nearby predator when barely hurt, not more. What the figure does not contain is any sign that the two slices diverge as injury rises, which is the interaction the interoceptive claim predicts.

1d · The five questions the sensor ladder asks of every agent

Everything above measures one thing: whether the agent's decision to step into cover changes with how badly it is hurt. That is the question this study pre-registered, and the answer is no. But the earlier sensory study asks five further questions of every agent it has — how long it lives, how much of its life it spends hidden, which of the three ways of dying it actually dies of, how its hiding changes as a predator closes in, and whether it can tell a predator from a harmless rabbit. None of those is about internal state, and none of them had been asked of this grid.

They are asked here by running the sensory study's own code over this grid's runs, not by writing new code that resembles it. The sweep that produced the ladder's numbers was given a list saying which run and which stored episodes belong to each of these twenty-one agents, and nothing else about it changed; it was re-checked against its own archived output on three ladder agents first, reproducing every field exactly, so a difference below cannot be a difference in the measuring instrument.

How to read every number in this section

The level a measure sits at is compared against t1none — the agent in this same grid, trained on the same day with the same code and the same seed, identical in every respect except that it has no modulator. The spread that counts as ordinary is taken from the five reference runs, because five runs is the only estimate of run-to-run variation this study has. Those two jobs are deliberately given to different runs: section 1b showed the five reference runs sit at a different level from this grid for reasons still unknown, which makes their average unusable as a yardstick for level but leaves their spread perfectly usable.

One consequence is easy to miss. A spread estimated from five runs is itself uncertain, so a "two standard deviations" line is far weaker here than the phrase suggests: with nothing whatever going on, about one cell in seven lands beyond it, and across sixteen cells the largest value is beyond three about half the time. Every single-cell number in this section is inside that range. They are reported because leaving them out would be hiding them, not because any one of them is a result.

What these five figures establish, and the one pattern worth a second look

No cell and no input-slice group is distinguishable from the unmodulated agent on any of these measures. Read against t1none with the five-run spread as the yardstick, every group difference is under two standard deviations. The largest single-cell values are exactly what sixteen draws against a five-run spread produce when nothing is going on. Every survival difference sits inside the band this study pre-registered as "no difference" — under 15 steps — before any of these numbers existed. And survival, hiding, and cause of death move together across these runs, closely enough to be one measure rather than four.

One exploratory pattern is worth a replication, and only that. Comparing the two restricted modulators at the same site — which cancels the batch problem entirely, because no external reference is involved — the modulator that reads only the outside world hides less and survives longer than the one that reads only the body at all five sites (mean +3.4 steps), and the body-only modulator answers a nearby predator less strongly at all five sites (mean 3.2 percentage points weaker).

Why that is a hint and not a result. Five sites is the smallest sample a sign test can run on: five out of five in one direction gives p = 0.06, which is not evidence, it is the best a five-item test can possibly do. The survival and hiding halves are the same axis, so this is one pattern and not two. And the previous figure shows that the five unmodulated seeds trace the same hiding-versus-survival line by themselves — so "five draws that happened to land at the low-hiding end of ordinary seed variation" fits these numbers as well as "reading the world causes it". The everything cells also read the world channels, and they sit with the body-only cells and the control on every one of these measures, which is not what a "reading the world causes it" story predicts.

Nothing here shows the modulator changes behaviour. It says that if it does, the body-versus-world contrast is where to look. That was written before the check below existed; the check has since been run, and it closes the question.

The pattern was checked against a second grid, and it did not survive

This project trained a twin of the entire sixteen-cell grid that differs in one respect: how the agent estimates the future value of what it is doing. The original grid adds up what actually happened for the rest of the episode; the twin uses the standard smoothed estimate instead. Everything else — the environment, the architecture, the budget, the evaluation worlds — is identical. If reading the body rather than the world genuinely changes an agent's behaviour, that should not depend on which of two standard bookkeeping methods was used to train it. Those sixteen runs finished on 2026-09-07; their million-episode evaluations were collected on 2026-09-08 and put through the same sweep, and this is the result.

Each row is the world-only modulator minus the body-only modulator at the same site, averaged over the five sites. "Sites agreeing" counts how many of the five point the same way as the original grid's average. No external reference run is involved in any of these numbers, so the batch problem of section 1b cannot reach them.

Every one of the six either collapses towards zero or changes sign. The measure that looked strongest in the original grid — the body-only modulator answering a nearby predator less strongly, at all five sites — comes back in the twin pointing the other way, with one site of five agreeing. On the original grid alone the honest reading was "this could be five draws that happened to land together, or it could be real". The twin is a fresh set of draws, and the pattern is not in them.

What this does and does not settle. The twin is not a fresh seed — both grids train their cells from seed 42 — so this does not measure seed-to-seed variation directly. What it shows is that the pattern does not survive a change in a training detail that has nothing to do with what the modulator reads, which is the robustness a claim about what the modulator reads would have to have. The five-seed replication the design pre-registered would still be the stronger test, and it is no longer worth running for this purpose.

The twin grid deserves its own analysis on its own terms, and that is a separate job, not attempted here. The table above uses it for one narrow purpose: to ask whether the one pattern this page was tempted to report holds up. It does not.

Results

All sixteen cells trained to ten million episodes and were evaluated on a million episodes each, against five unmodulated control runs evaluated the same way. No modulator configuration produced an internal-state-dependent change in behaviour that can be told apart from an unmodulated agent. The section below gives the six reports in the order fixed before the numbers existed.

The measurement that told me my own test was broken

The grid contains its own unmodulated control — cell t1none, identical to the fifteen modulated cells in every respect except that it has no modulator. When the first version of this analysis flagged cells as “outside the control range”, the control cell was one of them.

That cannot be a property of the agent, so it is a property of the test. The range of five controls is a range, not a confidence interval: a sixth draw from the same distribution is the new minimum or maximum with probability 2/6 — about 33%. The observed rates were 31%, 25% and 6%. Every “outside the band” flag was noise, and the control cell is the proof.

The tables below therefore report a z against the control mean and spread instead. It is still five runs on the control side and one on each cell's side, so it screens rather than tests — but it does not manufacture findings.

1 · Does the modulator do anything at all?

No. On the pre-registered headline measure, every cell sits within 1.3 standard deviations of the unmodulated control mean, and the control cell itself sits at +1.1.

ΔB0 — change in the bush-entry decision between the lowest and highest band of randomised starting injury (0–25 against 50–100). Controls, five seeds: ΔB0 mean −0.187 sd 0.268; Δrest mean 19.77 sd 1.21 (corrected, see 1b); survival mean 166.3 sd 1.8.

2 · Body-only against world-only — the thesis test

This is the comparison the project's story rests on, and it is reported whichever way it comes out. It comes out flat.

On the headline measure, body-only and world-only differ by 0.020 percentage points — 0.08 of one control standard deviation. A modulator restricted to the agent's own body produces the same bush-entry behaviour as one restricted to the outside world, and both produce the same behaviour as no modulator at all. That is the flattest possible answer to the question this grid was built to ask.

3 · Which site, if any

No ranking is given, because none is supportable. On the headline measure the sixteen cells span 0.52 percentage points while the five controls alone span 0.68 — the whole grid is narrower than the noise in the thing it is measured against. Ordering cells under those conditions would be reporting the seed.

4 · The decomposition, which is where the real effect is

What injury actually changes

Across all twenty-one agents, waking up wounded changes the bush-entry decision by about 0.1 percentage points and the resting rate by about 30. The second effect is roughly three hundred times the first, and it is present in every cell, modulated or not.

This is the freeze-to-heal finding reproduced on a different agent family and a fresh million episodes per run. It is also the reason this study's headline measure is bush entry rather than bush occupancy: a measure of where the agent is would have reported that enormous resting effect as if it were a decision to hide.

So the honest description of what a wound does to this agent is: it makes it stop moving. It does not measurably change where it chooses to go when it does move, and no modulator configuration changed that.

5 · The modulator's own behaviour — not measured

Tier C of the plan asked for the modulator's internal statistics, to separate “this site does not help” from “this site never learned to do anything”. Those numbers are not in this report. They live in the training-time metrics rather than the trajectory stores, and pulling them is a separate job that has not been done.

Stated plainly because it matters for how far the null above can be pushed: this analysis found no change in behaviour it can tell apart from an unmodulated agent — which is not the same as establishing that there was none. With one seed per cell measured against a five-seed spread, a real effect smaller than that spread would look exactly like this. It also does not establish why. A dead modulator and a working-but-useless one look identical from here, and telling them apart is the obvious next step.

6 · Exploratory — the one place with any structure

On survival, world-only modulators come out +3.4 steps above body-only ones (170.0 against 166.5), which is 1.9 control standard deviations. Four of the five world-only cells are in the top six survivors; the top cell overall, t16quad_X, sits at z = +2.8.

Why this is not a finding, and what would make it one

Three reasons to hold it loosely. It is one seed per cell. The design pre-registered thresholds of 15 and 30 survival steps; the entire spread across all sixteen cells is 7.7 steps, so nothing here comes close to clearing a bar that was set before the data existed. And it points the opposite way to the project's thesis — if it survived replication it would say the modulator's benefit comes from re-reading the outside world, not from listening to the body.

That last property is exactly why it is reported rather than quietly dropped. An exploratory signal that contradicts the hypothesis is worth more than one that flatters it, and this one is cheap to test: five seeds on t16quad_X and t16quad_I would settle it.

What this does and does not license

It licenses: that on a million paired episodes per agent, no combination of modulation site and input slice produced an internal-state-dependent change in the bush-entry decision distinguishable from an unmodulated agent, and that body-only and world-only modulators are indistinguishable from each other on that measure.

It does not license calling any cell eliminated. Every cell is one seed, and this study's own control cell demonstrated how easily one draw lands outside the range of five. A cell that failed to clear a threshold here is untested, not refuted — and that asymmetry was written into the plan before any number existed, precisely so it could not be renegotiated now.

It does not license a claim about why. The modulators may have been inert, or active but behaviourally irrelevant; nothing measured here separates those.

What would make the next round decisive

The reviewer's staged alternative, recorded in the design as still open, buys replication on every comparison for the same number of GPU slots: five write sites at three seeds, then the two survivors crossed with the input slices at three seeds. Given that this grid returned a clean null at n = 1, and that its one suggestive signal — the world-only survival edge — needs exactly that replication to mean anything, the case for the staged version is now stronger than it was when it was declined.

2 · The twin grid, and what the return estimator does

The same sixteen cells, the same control, the same five reference runs, the same environment and the same ten-million-episode budget — trained a second time with one thing changed. Every agent has to guess how good its current situation is. The first grid works that out by adding up what actually happened for the rest of the episode; the twin uses the standard smoothed estimate instead. That choice is bookkeeping internal to training. It should not change what kind of animal comes out.

This section asks two questions of the twin. First, the study's own question again: does the modulator do anything, under a second estimator? Second, and separately: what does swapping the estimator itself do? The second question turns out to have the only properly replicated answer anywhere on this page, and it is worth being clear about why.

Why this one comparison is different from every other on this page

Everywhere else, each cell of the grid is a single training run, so a difference between two cells could be the design or could be the dice. The estimator comparison is not like that. The five unmodulated reference runs were trained twice — once under each estimator — on the same day, from the same five seeds, from configuration files that differ in exactly one substantive setting. Five runs against five runs, one variable, same batch. That is a real comparison with a real error bar, and it is the only one here.

It also means the two questions in this section carry different weight, and the page should not let them borrow each other's confidence: the modulator answer is still one seed per cell, and the estimator answer is five against five.

2a · The pre-registered answer, asked again

The measure this study was built on is ΔB0 — how much the agent's decision to step into cover changes between waking up barely hurt and waking up badly hurt. Under the first estimator, no cell moved it. Under the twin, no cell moves it either.

Each group is the average of its five modulation sites, measured against the five reference runs of its own grid, in units of those five runs' spread.

On the headline measure the null replicates cleanly. Under both estimators every input-slice group sits within one standard deviation of its own controls, and the most extreme of the sixteen cells reaches 1.3 in each grid — which is what sixteen single runs measured against a five-run spread produce when nothing is happening.

The second row is the more instructive one. Under Monte-Carlo returns all three groups sat above their controls on the resting measure, by 1.5 to 2.1 standard deviations — the kind of consistent, modest, all-pointing-the-same-way pattern that is easy to write up as a finding. Under the twin the same three groups sit at −0.8 to +0.2. And the single most extreme cell is a different cell in each grid: the everything-reading encoder in the first, the body-reading encoder in the second. A real effect does not move house between estimators.

2b · What swapping the estimator actually does

Now the other question, on the five-against-five comparison. Three of the seven measures move, and the largest of them is not what it first looks like.

± is the standard deviation across the five seeds. The bottom two rows are the two halves of the “response to a nearby predator” contrast used elsewhere on this page.

The number that means the opposite of what it looks like

The contrast this page uses for threat response — hiding with a predator close, minus hiding with none near — is 5.5 percentage points larger under the twin. Read at face value that says the GAE agent answers a predator more strongly. It does not.

Split into its two halves, the near term does not move at all: 46.8% against 47.5%, a difference of six tenths of a point that five seeds cannot distinguish from zero. The entire difference is in the far term. When nothing is hunting it, the Monte-Carlo agent is in a bush on a quarter of its steps and the GAE agent on a fifth — 4.9 points less, and that gap is larger than the seed-to-seed spread.

So the twin's agent is not more frightened of predators. It is less inclined to sit in cover when there is nothing to hide from. Its hiding is more selective, not stronger. A contrast reported on its own would have carried the wrong mechanism into everything downstream of it, and this is the second time on this page that a difference of differences has had to be taken apart before it could be read.

The survival difference is not new. The twin's agents live about 4.6 steps longer, and an earlier study on these same ten checkpoints reported +4.5 from a smaller evaluation. The million-episode sweep sharpens that number by removing world-sampling noise; it adds no seeds, so the strength of the claim is unchanged. It is a re-measurement, not a second result.

How the agent dies does not change at all. The three ways an episode can end — killed, starved, ran out of time — are within a tenth of a point of each other across the two estimators. Whatever changed, it did not change the balance of the two dangers.

What the predator-contrast result is worth. All five GAE runs sit above all five Monte-Carlo runs, and so do the fifteen modulated cells and the in-grid control of each grid — 21 against 21 with no overlap. The formal test lands at about p = 0.007, which is exactly on the line once seven measures are accounted for. The sixteen cells are not independent replicates — they share a seed and a training batch — so this is a consistency check rather than a second sample. It is a strong one, and it is still five seeds against five.

2c · What this does not settle about hiding and survival

Within these grids, hiding predicts survival under one estimator and not the other: a slope of −2.4 steps per point of hiding (95% confidence interval −3.5 to −1.3) under Monte-Carlo, holding separately in the sixteen cells and in the five controls, and +0.2 (interval −1.4 to +1.8) under the twin, holding in neither. The Monte-Carlo relationship is carried almost entirely by how much each agent idles in cover when no predator is near — the same quantity the twin compresses.

Why that is not a retraction of the sensor ladder's finding

The earlier sensory study reported that agents which hide more die sooner, as a property of a world where bushes are safe and contain no food. It is tempting to read the paragraph above as overturning it. It cannot, for a reason that has nothing to do with statistics: these grids do not cover the range that result lives in. The ladder's fourteen agents span 14.0% to 20.2% hiding and 166 to 264 survival steps. Every agent on this page, both grids together, spans 13.2% to 15.5% hiding and 163 to 175 steps — about a third of the ladder's hiding range and a twelfth of its survival range.

Nor could it: the ladder's agents were all trained under Monte-Carlo returns, so what a sensory ladder would do under the other estimator is simply not a thing anyone has measured. And the mechanism the ladder named — a bush is safe and has no food in it — is a fact about the environment that the estimator cannot touch. The honest statement is the narrow one: inside the two-point hiding range these grids occupy, the correlation is present under one estimator and absent under the other, and the wider claim is untested either way.

2d · A reference problem, stated rather than routed around

Section 1b established that the five reference runs sit at a different level from the grid, and that the grid's own control — t1none — is therefore the right yardstick for level. In the twin that rule has a visible cost. Measured against its five same-configuration siblings, the twin's t1none is itself unusual: +2.3 standard deviations on hiding, +2.7 on the predator contrast, +3.0 on the rabbit contrast — while the fifteen modulated cells sit at the reference level.

That matters because it changes what a table says depending on which reference it uses. Measured against t1none, the twin's everything-reading group looks like it is 3.3 standard deviations low on threat response. Measured against the five reference runs, the same group is at −0.6, and the gap is between that one control run and its own siblings rather than between the modulated cells and anything. Against the reference mean, every modulated group in both grids sits within one standard deviation on all seven measures, with two exceptions at about 2.3.

Both readings are reported here rather than one being chosen, because with a single run on one side and five on the other there is no way to tell whether t1none drew an unusual seed or whether the batch difference of section 1b is showing up again on a different set of measures. The five-run spread that the standard deviations are quoted in is itself estimated from five numbers, so it carries a wide interval of its own — on the twin's predator contrast the true spread could plausibly be anywhere from about half to nearly three times the value used. Every standard deviation on this page inherits that uncertainty.

What the twin grid adds, in three sentences

The study's answer does not depend on the estimator. No modulator configuration produced a detectable change in the pre-registered measure under either return estimator, and the one modest pattern the first grid offered — the resting measure sitting above the controls for all three input slices — does not survive the second.

The estimator itself does change the agent, and in a specific way. On the only five-against-five comparison this study contains, the GAE-trained agent lives about 4.6 steps longer and spends about 5 percentage points less of its time in cover when nothing is hunting it, while hiding just as much when something is. How it dies does not change.

The relationship between hiding and survival differs between the two grids, and that is as far as it goes. It is a statement about a two-point range of hiding, not about the world, and the sensory study's much wider finding is neither confirmed nor contradicted by it.

3 · Low wound against high wound — and where this study sits on the sensory ladder

The sensory study's sharpest causal test asks one question: hand the agent a wound it did nothing to earn, and see whether it hides more. Thirteen of its fourteen agents did, by 2.6 to 6.7 percentage points. One did not. This section asks the same question of all forty-two runs in the neuromodulator study. No modulator changes the answer — and the answer itself places this study on the one rung of that ladder whose early-window response is negative, which a diagnosis written four days before the grid launched had already worked out from the configuration alone.

Why a dealt wound is the one internal state that proves anything

Everywhere else, a wounded agent is a suspicious comparison: it got hurt by doing something, so whatever it does next is contaminated by whatever it was doing when it got hurt. This environment removes that. At the start of every episode the agent is handed an injury drawn uniformly from 0 to 100 before it has acted at all. Behaviour that tracks that number was caused by it, full stop.

The measurement window is the first 25 steps, and it is the sensory study's choice rather than one made here: the wound heals as the episode runs, so averaging over a whole episode dilutes the dose the environment dealt with whatever the agent's own later behaviour produced. Both windows are reported below so the dilution is visible rather than asserted.

What the study shares with that ladder arm, stated exactly

Every one of the forty-two runs was trained in the same world as the ladder's A_baseline agent — same environment, same sensors (a single omnidirectional whiff of smell, sight of one cell), same nociceptor. Beyond the environment the runs differ from that agent by known amounts, and the difference is not the same for all of them:

  • the five Monte-Carlo reference runs are that agent exactly — their saved configurations differ from its own only in the run's name and its logging labels;
  • the five GAE reference runs add one setting, the return estimator;
  • the two in-grid controls add a critic learning rate that, as section 1b records, no code in the repository reads;
  • the thirty modulated cells add that same inert value plus the modulator itself.

So “identical configuration” is a claim about five runs, not forty-two. What all forty-two share is the environment — and on this measure that is what appears to matter, since the sign does not move across any of those differences.

The environment was chosen deliberately, and the connection was already made. The grid's design picked this setting for continuity with the earlier return-mode study, recorded its zero sensor ranges in its own table, and noted before launch that its unmodulated controls leaned the wrong way. A diagnosis written on 2026-09-03 — four days before the grid launched — had already identified this agent as functionally the ladder's A_baseline twin and called the negative sign “not a coincidence”. Nothing here is a discovery of an oversight; the figure is the first time the two populations have been measured side by side through one code path.

How much replication there actually is

It is tempting to say the ladder's lone A_baseline result now has ten more runs behind it. It has four. The ladder's agent ran at seed 42, and so does this study's baseline_s42 — same configuration, same seed, and as it happens the same node and the same card. That pair is a repeat, not a replicate; the two came out at −2.34 and −2.90, which incidentally shows this stack is not bit-reproducible even given all of that.

The genuine fresh seeds of the identical configuration are four: −1.63, −4.14, −2.90 and −1.57. Beyond them sit the same five seeds under the other return estimator (−1.84 to −2.79) and the two in-grid controls (−3.97 and −1.98). The sign holds in every one of the eleven, which is worth something; the replication proper is four seeds, and the page should not claim more.

What this does not explain

It is easy to reach for a mechanism here — that a poorly-sensed agent answers a wound by stopping where it stands rather than travelling to cover. Freezing to heal is certainly what these agents do; their resting rate climbs 17 to 29 percentage points across the injury range. But the sensory study found that same freezing in all fourteen of its agents, including the thirteen whose early-window sign is positive. A mechanism shared by both groups cannot be what separates them.

Nor is “it cannot find a bush” supported: A_baseline spends 15.9% of its steps in cover, squarely mid-pack in the ladder's 14.0–20.2% range. Why this configuration's early-window response runs negative while better-sensed ones run positive is not established by anything on this page. What the figure does establish is that no modulator, at any site, reading anything, moves it.

Design and pre-registration: docs/experiments/active/nmn_input_site_grid/NMN_INPUT_SITE_GRID.md.

The GAE_NORM twin grid finished training on 2026-09-07; its twenty-one runs were evaluated on 2026-09-08 over the same million worlds and analysed in section 2, from results/analysis/nmn_gaenorm_grid/. The ladder-style measures in sections 1d and 2 come from scripts/analysis/studies/sensor_ladder/collect_arm_data.py --manifest — the sensory study's own sweep, pointed at these runs rather than reimplemented; the estimator comparison is scripts/analysis/studies/nmn_site_grid/compare_estimators.py and the wound dose-response of section 3 is scripts/analysis/studies/nmn_site_grid/injury_dose_response.py. Design and pre-registration for the twin: docs/experiments/active/nmn_input_site_grid/NMN_INPUT_SITE_GRID_GAENORM.md.
